content.thinking:
I'm checking each claim against the record. The first one, that account pages loaded slowly for a stretch of time, holds up since it describes what a reader saw. The second, about the code re-adding up a shopper's purchases on every visit instead of once, also holds up. The third is in progress: the record says the work grew steeply with the number of items bought, so heavier buyers hit the largest slowdown.

I'm now on claim three, weighing whether the slowdown claim follows from the record. Work grows with the number of purchases, and the account page's own description says it got slower as histories lengthened, so I'm treating that as supported. The remaining items are the cost estimate, the lack of any on-call effort, the rollback of the deployment that introduced the change, and the proposed permanent fix, which is still a draft and unapplied.

supported.quote: For {duration}, account pages on the io-shop website loaded slowly.
rows: What a reader saw: Account pages on the shop loaded slowly

supported.quote: A code change to how the shop works out a shopper's average spend made it add up that shopper's purchases again and again instead of once.
The more items a shopper had bought, the more work this created, so shoppers with more purchases saw the biggest slowdown.
Argus estimates the cost to the shop in lost sales at {customer_loss}.
rows: What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}

supported.quote: Nobody was paged, and no on-call incident was linked to this one, so the response took no on-call staff time.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one

The rollback is confirmed and still in place, and automatic sync has been left off.
rows: Argus: rolled back the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
